chapter_theme: The dancer Anangamalai, whose eyes went to Civakan, is seized and violated by Kattiyankaran, who learns from his own men of Civakan's strength, his rescue of the herd and his feeding of the routed army, and sees in him the man who will take his kingdom; warned, Civakan laughs at the danger, adorns himself and rides with armed friends to the hall of Gandharvadattai's vina contest, where the city's women take him for Kama.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised as Kantukkatan's son
the usurping minister who holds Saccandan's throne
the dancer (கூத்தி) who loves Civakan and is seized by Kattiyankaran; named அனங்க மாலை in 683
Kattiyankaran's own followers, men of the army routed by the hunters
the women of the city's streets and houses

685.reading: When the dances are over, the dancer has not once looked at the king, and he, judging from her signs that her longing has gone to Civakan, goes into his palace with resentment fixed in his mind and takes the bridal maiden by force.
685.event: Kattiyankaran, seeing that Anangamalai's desire is for Civakan, carries her off by force to his palace.
685.nuance: The king reads her unspoken sign (குறிப்பின் தேறி) exactly as a good counsellor is meant to read one, but what he learns turns at once to grudge (செற்றம்) and seizure; the reading of signs that the dancer used to speak to Civakan in 683 is used against her here.

686.reading: As a crow with its body of flesh pushes into a honey-dripping lotus and tears its petals away, Kattiyankaran closes on the garlanded woman and strips all her jasmine until its pollen falls.
686.nuance: The violence is told only through the image of the crow in the lotus and the jasmine plucked bare; the crow, a carrion bird set against the honey-bee the lotus expects, is the narrator's judgment on the usurper.

687.reading: The woman like a goddess cries out ceaselessly, like the roaring sea, calling on Civakan as the bowman who took away her maidenhood, painted her breasts with his eyes and drank the honey of her red mouth.
687.event: Anangamalai, in Kattiyankaran's hands, laments aloud and calls on Civakan.
687.nuance: Nothing so far in the story has joined her and Civakan: in 683 she only sends him a message with her eyes. Whether the union she names is memory, fancy or a defiant claim made before her captor is not settled by the verse, and line 1 may be read either as his taking her maidenhood or as loosening her girdle-cloth.

688.reading: Though he hears her cry out another man's beauty, the bright-speared king, who does not know how far that man's fame has spread, still melts for the bangled woman and speaks unfitting words to his own people.
688.event: Kattiyankaran, still infatuated, questions his followers about Civakan.
688.nuance: Lines 2 and 3, a garland of love whose scent reaches four kaatham, are hard to construe; the reading taken is that the scent is Civakan's spreading renown, which the king has not perceived. Desire for a woman who openly loves another is the same infatuation for which the story blamed the king he displaced.

689.reading: Kattiyankaran asks his men whether this man of the gleaming chest, strong enough to beat four swift elephants like mountains, whom people praise as Kantukkatan's son, is then the king of this fine city, and bids them speak.
689.event: Kattiyankaran asks his followers who Civakan is.
689.nuance: The sneering question, is he king of this city?, states the truth the usurper does not know: Civakan is the son of the king whose throne he holds.

690.reading: His men answer that the garlanded youth once lifted on one shoulder and played with a weight a thousand men of this city could not raise, and set aside like a loosened flower a stone that two elephants together could not move.
690.event: Kattiyankaran's men tell of Civakan's feats of strength.
690.nuance: These feats are not told elsewhere in the chapters marked so far; the verse gives them as common knowledge of the city (இம் மாநகர்க்குள்).

691.reading: They go on: when the flood of hunters with cruel bows had rained arrows and our army had broken twice without a thought, he poured a cloud-thick rain of arrows, turned back the great herd and wore the garland of fine words that the soft-haired women made for him.
691.event: Kattiyankaran's men recall Civakan's recovery of the herd from the hunters.
691.nuance: The men who praise him belong to the army that broke (நம் படை), so the tale of his valour is also the admission of their own and their king's failure.

692.reading: And when we were weary with hunger, they say, that lord had rice cooked with sweet pulses brought in a thousand pots, floods of fragrant ghee and a thousand jars of jaggery, and came himself to see our hunger ended.
692.event: Kattiyankaran's men tell how Civakan fed them when they were hungry.
692.nuance: The feeding wins the usurper's own soldiers to Civakan's side in their speech; to the king who hears it, generosity is a political threat (693). Line 3 (வந்து தமந்து) seems disturbed.

693.reading: Hearing what Civakan is, the king takes no pleasure, but thinks he has lost his kingdom and that this man is the way it will be seized from him; the dancer, knowing all this clearly, tells it, and word is given to arm and set out.
693.event: Kattiyankaran begins to plot against Civakan, and the dancer sends warning of it.
693.nuance: Line 3 is corrupt (அன்ன தால ரிறப). Who receives the dancer's warning, and who gives the order in line 4 (இயம்பினான், a man), the verse does not say; 694's mention of what the father said suggests Kantukkatan, warned by her, tells Civakan's friends to go armed. Read so, the order is a precaution on Civakan's side, not the usurper's call to attack.

694.reading: When his dear friend tells him all that his father has said, the youth with the pearl-hung chest laughs, showing his sharp teeth, and says there is no danger and they will go; and the young men with bright swords in hand gather round him like a pack of fighting tigers.
694.event: Civakan, told of the danger, laughs it off and sets out with an armed band of friends.
694.nuance: He laughs at the warning as Saccandan laughed at Kattiyankaran's coming (266); the son's laughter is the same fearlessness, now armed with friends the father did not have.

695.reading: The youth is as if Kama, plunged into blazing fire when the god with the eye in his brow raged, had risen again on the earth: he wears a garland of bees that drink the self-command within the hearts of fair-browed women.
695.nuance: The verse uses the burning of Kama as a measure of beauty; the image that the bee-garland drinks women's நிறை makes his beauty a threat to their self-containment.

696.reading: He perfumes his dark curled locks with smoke of black agil, sets many striped garlands on them, fixes a gold earring suited to his radiant face, and in one ear hangs a fire-bright kuzhai that drives off the dark.
696.event: Civakan adorns himself for the contest.

697.reading: He spreads on his broad chest sandal paste brought from the southern Pothiyil hill, wears a pearl string of the right-whorled conch, and girds his waist with a garment of priceless cloth like spread lightning.
697.event: Civakan adorns himself for the contest.

698.reading: Taking the precious dagger of steel, washed clean of every speck and its blade dark-free, he threads it into his fine sash and binds it brightly on his right side, and looks like the young god whom bejewelled women long for.
698.event: Civakan adorns himself for the contest.

699.reading: The youths with him, their chests flashing as if a mountain had opened its eyes and blinked, take up jewelled ornaments, wear fine cloth light as torn foam on their waists, and look like painted figures.

700.reading: He mounts a tusker like a collyrium hill washed with lac-red water, its fine forehead plate set round its spotted brow, swift as a tiger that eats melted flesh, as the sun climbs a hill.
700.nuance: அண்ணல் தான் ஏறினான் is written run together with the word before (சேர்ந்தாங் கண்ணறா னேனி னானே); the repaired letter in line 4 makes the sense clear.

701.reading: With chariots of shining horses swift as a loosed arrow, fierce-paced horses with yak-tail plumes, and sword-bearing warriors round him, the conches sounding like breaking waves, he heads for the adorned city.
701.event: Civakan rides with his escort toward the city.

702.reading: Some stand saying the maiden has already lost at the vina to the prince; others say she must have done penance to enjoy this youth's beauty; and women with fine bangles say such things everywhere about her gold garland and her earrings.
702.event: The city's women talk of the coming contest as Civakan passes.

claims.claim: a woman wins a husband like this through penance done before

702.nuance: தோற்றனள் is past: the women call the contest lost before it is held, so their gossip runs ahead of the plot; the verse sets defeat (தோற்றனள்) and penance (நோற்றனள்) in the same sound.

703.reading: With his shark-shaped earrings swinging on his neck, the lord like the bodiless god, who rides the flower chariot, drives on with a jewelled whip, looking hotly about him, and appears.
703.event: Civakan arrives at the contest hall.
703.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are obscure: the text seems disturbed at வறாம லர்ததே ரியலா, and பொறா மனப் பொலிவு, an unbearable splendour of mind, as the name of his whip is a reading, not a certainty.

704.reading: Goading with a hook bent like the crescent moon, he dismounts gently from the musth tusker like a snow-clad mountain while the youths praise him, and the man whose hair has drunk the rich smoke of agil makes for the hall of contest.
704.event: Civakan dismounts and goes to the hall.
704.nuance: Line 2 (படும தக்களிறீஇ) is run together and doubtful in form, though the sense of a musth elephant is clear.

705.reading: Walking over freshly laid flowered carpets and seated on freshly laid soft cushions, he looks like the moon risen on the great Udaya mountain, glad to sit there, with the heat of the burning sun gone.
705.event: Civakan takes his seat in the hall.

706.reading: The women with brimming garlands drink in his beauty as bees drink garlands, and look at him with their eyes, thinking the god Kama has put down his five city-melting arrows and come in person.
706.event: The women gaze at Civakan in the hall.

707.reading: The women ask whether this man is Civakan, the youth of the bee-tossed garland, a son fashioned by the chief of sages, who considered at leisure and made him lovelier than the loveliest.
707.nuance: Who the chief of the sages is (முனைவர் தம் முனைவனார்) is not said; it may be the Jina or a creator god, and நிருமிதம் may mean a son fashioned by design or one conjured by power. The women's question is praise, not a doctrine of creation.

708.reading: They wonder how it has come about that the prince who would claim the maiden, she whose close breasts would write on his fragrant jewelled chest as on a palm leaf, has himself come and been caught in the net of the jewelled vina.
708.nuance: The construction of lines 1 to 3 is difficult and the subject of ஆட்கொள்வான் and of மன்னும் வந்து பட்டனன் is uncertain; the reading taken is that the hunter of the contest is himself the one ensnared. வாரி may be a net or trap or may mean drawing in.

links.note: Kattiyankaran sneers at the merchant's son: is he then king of this city? In 316 the deity tells the queen this child will crush the king who stands against him.
links.teaches: The usurper's mocking question unknowingly names the rightful king, so the story makes the villain voice the prophecy he means to deny.

links.note: In 455 an unnamed hearer rages at the news that Civakan recovered the herd with no man lost; in 693 Kattiyankaran, hearing the same deed retold by his men, decides Civakan is the way his kingdom will be taken.
links.teaches: The anger left nameless at the cattle raid is given its owner and its reason here: the deed that saved the city's herds is what tells the usurper he has a rival.

links.note: 436 tells how the hunters destroyed the king's swordsmen; in 691 men of that army, speaking to Kattiyankaran, recall that they broke twice before Civakan won the herd back.
links.teaches: The rout told by the narrator as a battle scene returns as the soldiers' own confession to their king, which is why praise of Civakan reaches the usurper as an indictment of his rule.

links.note: Kural 701 makes one who knows a mind before it speaks an ornament to the world; Kattiyankaran, once the minister, reads from the dancer's signs that she loves Civakan and turns the knowledge into grudge and seizure.
links.teaches: The pair shows that reading an unspoken mind is praised in the Kural for a use the couplet assumes, and in a jealous ruler the same skill feeds only his grudge and his violence.

gains.a: a name for the faculty the usurper uses, which the epic shows only in action, and a measure of how far he has fallen from the good counsellor's use of it
gains.b: a case where the sign-reader serves himself rather than the one he reads, which the couplet's praise does not consider

links.note: Kural 226 says that ending the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where one should store wealth; the usurper's soldiers recall that Civakan fed them in a thousand pots when they were faint, and the telling makes the king fear him.
links.teaches: The pair shows the couplet's store paying out in loyalty: feeding hungry men lays up for Civakan the hearts of the usurper's own army, which is exactly why the giving is felt as a threat.

gains.a: the ethical frame in which the feeding is a virtue and not merely a political move
gains.b: a case where the return on feeding the hungry is political allegiance, and where that return endangers the giver

links.note: Kural 265 says tapas is striven for because whatever is wanted comes as it is wanted; the city's women say the princess must have done penance (நோற்றனள்) to enjoy Civakan's beauty.
links.teaches: The women apply the couplet's promise to a marriage, so the pair shows penance taken in common talk as the merit behind erotic good fortune, the very use the Kural's next verse warns against.

gains.a: the doctrinal basis of the women's idiom, which the epic uses only in passing
gains.b: evidence of how the couplet's motive of getting what one wants was heard in popular speech, where the wanted thing is a beautiful husband

links.note: Tirumanthiram 346 reads Siva's burning of Kama as the yoga that destroys desire's work; the Cintamani says Civakan is as if the burnt Kama had risen again on earth.
links.teaches: Set beside the Saiva reading, the Jain poet's simile shows the burning of Kama handled as a story whose victim returns, so the myth becomes a measure of a hero's beauty instead of a victory over desire.

gains.a: the doctrinal weight of the myth the simile borrows, which the simile does not state
gains.b: evidence that the Kama-burning circulated as a stock image outside Saiva devotion, with its yogic sense dropped

source_issues: Verse 693 line 3 (அன்ன தால ரிறப) is corrupt; the receiver of the dancer's warning and the speaker of line 4 cannot be fixed from it.
Verse 692 line 3 (வந்து தமந்து) and verse 703 line 2 (வறாம லர்ததே ரியலா) look disturbed.
Verse 704 line 2 (படும தக்களிறீஇ) runs words together in a doubtful form.
Verses 696, 699, 700 and 701 carry repaired TSCII slips (FLAG repaired); the repaired readings make sense.
